blogs.title: "Similarity" in the Eye of the Beholder: The Federal Circuit Demands Doctrinal Consistency Across DuPont Factors
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Federal Circuit's core holding that the TTAB cannot apply inconsistent definitions of "similarity" across different DuPont factors. The court held that when the Board found the parties' services "highly similar" and even "legally identical, in part" under the second DuPont factor, it was legal error to narrow the universe of third-party marks considered under the sixth factor to only those used for credit card services—excluding marks for other banking and financial services. The post explores the broader implications of this consistency requirement for multi-factor balancing tests: Does this ruling constrain the Board's ability to calibrate the scope of inquiry under each factor? And does it signal that the Federal Circuit views the DuPont factors as more interdependent than previously understood, where a factual finding under one factor effectively constrains the analytical framework of another?

blogs.title: The Cascade Effect: How Errors in DuPont Factor Six Can Reshape Factor One's Commercial Impression Analysis
blogs.description: This post examines the Federal Circuit's decision to vacate the first DuPont factor analysis (similarity of the marks) based solely on its vacatur of the sixth factor (third-party marks and mark weakness). The court reasoned that because reconsideration of the sixth factor "may result in a different determination of the mark's commercial strength or weakness," the Board must also revisit the first factor's commercial impression analysis. The post discusses the doctrinal significance of this cascade effect: the court appears to treat commercial strength as a thread that runs through multiple factors, linking the sixth factor's assessment of mark weakness to the first factor's evaluation of overall commercial impression. The post considers whether this interdependence creates a risk of circularity in DuPont analysis and how practitioners should approach the strategic presentation of evidence on commercial strength given this cascading relationship.

blogs.title: How Many Marks Make a Crowd? The Elusive Quantum for Demonstrating Mark Weakness Under DuPont Factor Six
blogs.description: This post focuses on the substantive question of how much third-party use is sufficient to establish that a mark is weak and entitled to only a narrow scope of protection. The Board found that nine third-party uses of "Aspire" in connection with credit card services did not rise to the level of "considerable" or "ubiquitous" use, citing prior Federal Circuit cases that involved significantly larger numbers of marks (fourteen in Jack Wolfskin, twenty-six in Juice Generation). The post analyzes the emerging jurisprudence on the quantum question: Is there a numerical threshold, or is the inquiry inherently context-dependent? The post also examines the tension between the Board's acknowledgment that CC Serve had not shown its mark to be commercially strong and its simultaneous refusal to find the mark weak—leaving the mark in a doctrinal middle ground of "normal scope of protection." The remand, which expands the universe of potentially relevant third-party marks beyond credit card services, may push the total number of marks the Board must consider above the thresholds cited in prior cases, potentially reshaping the calculus.
